messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Anjali Patel was 44 when she sought treatment, a married South Asian American woman who had spent years working the sales floor at a large discount store. The trauma she returned to in fragments was the day she witnessed a customer collapse during a chaotic rush near the front registers. A woman had begun crying hard while arguing on the phone, swayed, and fell. Anjali remembered the sound of a basket hitting the floor, people shouting for help, and the woman’s body looking suddenly wrong and still. What stayed with her most was the crying just before the collapse and the helplessness of standing nearby, watching others crowd in while she froze, lightheaded and unable to take in what was happening. Even now, when she tries to tell the story, she loses the order of it—whether the crying came before the fall or after the shouting started—and the confusion itself unsettles her.

In the weeks afterward, ordinary moments at work began to pull the memory back with alarming force. If a customer started crying at a register, Anjali felt the scene rush up whole in feeling but not in sequence. If she became dizzy from standing too long under the bright lights, that bodily sensation seemed to transport her back to the moment she thought she might faint. Being asked by her husband or a coworker to explain what had happened was often just as potent; as soon as she tried to talk about it, she was flooded by grief and had to stop, pressing her lips together as if words themselves might undo her. The memory had become both easily provoked and hard to hold onto in an organized way, surfacing as an emotional blow more than a coherent account. Once it was living in her this way, Anjali began to find pieces of it everywhere; after a bad spell of remembering, the sound of someone crying, the glare of the front lights, even a brief wave of dizziness no longer felt neutral but charged, as if the memory itself had taught her what to notice and fear.

When the memory returned, Anjali did not simply feel upset; she felt overcome. She described a wave of grief so strong that she had to sit down or leave the room, and because she could not place the moments in the right order, she kept circling back to them, trying to understand what exactly she had seen and why it had happened in front of her. She found herself dwelling on the question of why this event had happened to her, as if there must be some explanation that would settle her. At the same time, she began adjusting herself around other people. At work she became more agreeable, saying yes to shift changes, extra tasks, and customer demands with very little resistance, because going along with what others wanted made her feel less exposed and less likely to face conflict or emotion she could not manage. The more overwhelming and disorganized the memory felt, the more she relied on these habits to get through the day.

That same disjointed, grief-laden recall also left her feeling persistently unsafe. Anjali had come to feel that danger could appear without warning, the way it had in the store aisle. She became superalert in crowded places, scanning faces, hands, and movements for signs that someone might suddenly collapse or that some crisis was about to unfold again. Small noises made her jump. In those keyed-up moments, the event came back more readily, as though staying on guard kept pulling her mind toward the woman on the floor; the more danger she felt around her, the less the scene stayed in the past and the more vividly it returned. On the sales floor, she often caught herself watching customers more than she was stocking shelves, tracking who looked unsteady, who sounded distressed, who might need help before something terrible happened. Because the memory remained incomplete and overpowering, it never felt fully in the past; it behaved as if it were still a live possibility.

Over months, this watchfulness fed directly into the ways she tried to cope. The more on guard she felt, the more she checked her surroundings, sweeping the store entrance, register lines, and endcaps for signs of trouble. Her people-pleasing intensified too; if a manager asked her to handle an upset customer, she complied immediately, not because she felt confident, but because refusing felt dangerous. She believed that keeping others calm and satisfied might prevent another scene. Yet these efforts did not settle her. Constant scanning kept her body tense and her attention fixed on possible danger, and that state of tension made the memory easier to trigger. A crying customer, a spell of lightheadedness, or a simple question about the event could again bring the grief and confusion crashing back.

The cycle had grown tighter by the time she came for help. Her checking of the environment meant she noticed every small sign of distress in the store, and each noticed sign carried the memory closer to the surface. Her attempts to think through why it had happened only pulled her deeper into the same disordered recollections, and once those recollections surged, she became more jumpy and more vigilant. At home, her husband had grown used to seeing her fall silent when he asked about difficult days; sometimes she would start to speak, tear up, and stop mid-sentence, shaken and ashamed that she still could not tell the story straight. She finally sought treatment after nearly leaving the sales floor when a customer began sobbing near the checkout and Anjali became so dizzy and overwhelmed that she had to hide in the stockroom. What frightened her most was the sense that she was no longer in charge of her own mind—that a sound, a question, or a feeling in her body could pull her back instantly—and what she most hoped for was to be able to remember what happened without falling apart in the middle of an ordinary workday.
